stories.title: AMD unveils CPU-only Helion rack to support agentic AI workloads
stories.summary: Chip designer working with ecosystem partners ahead of planned November launch date
stories.why_it_matters: A credible CPU-only rack challenges the assumption that every AI workload needs GPUs, which could reshape procurement economics for inference-heavy deployments. If ecosystem partners coalesce around Helion, AMD gains a differentiated wedge in the AI infrastructure market where Nvidia currently dominates, potentially easing supply pressure and opening new colocation configurations.
stories.title_zh: AMD发布仅CPU的Helion机架以支持agentic AI工作负载
stories.content:
AMD has unveiled Helion, a CPU-only rack designed to support agentic AI workloads.

Announced by AMD at the OCP Global Summit in San Jose today (October 12), the company said Helion builds on the “open-platform approach” of its Helios rackscale solution, which was launched earlier this year.

Designed for hyperscale customers, Helion is powered by 6th Gen AMD Epyc 'Venice' server CPUs, supporting up to 32,768 CPU cores. However, AMD said users can customize the rack’s configurations by integrating CPU and AMD Instinct GPU nodes in order to match agent execution, model inference, and tailor compute to each deployment’s performance, power, and cost needs.

Available in both liquid and air-cooled versions, AMD says this approach allows users to “create virtually any configuration needed” to support their requirements.

“Agentic AI is not a single workload. It spans personal agents, enterprise applications, code execution and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements,” said Dan McNamara, SVP and GM, compute and enterprise AI, AMD. “To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing AMD Epyc performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power.”

AMD said it plans to contribute its Helion specification to OCP, making it available to the community for further development and adoption. At present, the Helion agentic rack configurations are still under development with ecosystem partners, but AMD expects them to be available in November 2026

Ecosystem partners working with AMD for Helion’s launch include Cisco, Dell, Hon Hai Technology (aka Foxconn), HPE, Lenovo, Supermicro, and Wiwynn.
stories.why_zh: 一款可信的纯CPU机架挑战了每个AI工作负载都需要GPU的假设，这可能重塑面向推理密集型部署的采购经济性。如果生态合作伙伴围绕Helion形成合力，AMD将在目前由Nvidia主导的AI基础设施市场中获得一个差异化的切入点，有望缓解供应压力，并开辟新的colocation配置方案。

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): MN Holdings Bhd (KL:MNHLDG) has secured a RM293.88 million contract to build two high-voltage power facilities for a data centre development in the central region of Peninsular Malaysia.

In a bourse filing on Monday, the infrastructure utilities construction and engineering group said its wholly-owned MN Power Transmission Sdn Bhd had accepted a letter of award (LOA) from an undisclosed Malaysian company involved in providing infrastructure for hosting, data processing and related services.

The exact location of the project was also not disclosed.

The contract involves the construction of two 275-kilovolt (kV) consumer landing stations.

Under the contract, MN Power Transmission will undertake the construction, supply, installation, testing and commissioning of the facilities, including main buildings and related external works.

Construction began in September 2026 and is expected to be completed by August 2027.

MN Holdings executive director Datuk Dang Siong Diang said the contract reflected continued demand for high-voltage power infrastructure to support large-scale data centre developments in Malaysia.

"Our experience in delivering high-voltage substations and power infrastructure positions us well to participate in this growing segment, and we remain focused on executing these projects effectively while continuing to pursue opportunities across the power infrastructure, data centre and utilities sectors across Peninsular Malaysia," he said in a statement.

As at end-June 2026, MN Holdings had an outstanding order book of RM1.64 billion, with projects across the power, renewable energy, data centre and water infrastructure segments.

The group recently closed its financial year ended June 30, 2026 with a near doubling of annual profit to a record RM92.14 million, as revenue jumped 60.8% to RM869.19 million.

This comes as it reported a 98.8% surge in its fourth-quarter net profit to RM23.98 million from RM12.06 million a year earlier, driven by stronger contributions from its substation engineering segment and a reversal of impairment losses.

Quarterly revenue rose 17.9% to RM211.47 million from RM179.42 million, with the substation engineering segment recording a 24% increase in contribution on higher work progress and project activities.

MN Holdings shares rose three sen or 0.76% to close at RM3.96 on Monday, valuing the group at RM2.74 billion. The counted has gained more than 135% year to date.

stories.summary: IJM Corporation Bhd (KL:IJM) has secured a RM1.23 billion contract from AT&S Austria Technologie & Systemtechnik (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd to construct semiconductor manufacturing facilities at the Kulim Hi-Tech Park in Kedah.

stories.title_zh: IJM赢得12.3亿令吉合同，在吉打州为AT&S建设半导体制造设施
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): IJM Corporation Bhd (KL:IJM) has secured a RM1.23 billion contract from AT&S Austria Technologie & Systemtechnik (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd to construct semiconductor manufacturing facilities at the Kulim Hi-Tech Park in Kedah.

AT&S Malaysia is a subsidiary of Vienna-listed Austria Technologie & Systemtechnik AG (AT&S), an Austrian manufacturer of high-end printed circuit boards (PCBs) and integrated circuit (IC) substrates, which are used to connect semiconductor chips to circuit boards.

The Austrian group established its first Southeast Asian manufacturing campus in Kulim, where it began high-volume production of IC substrates for US chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc (AMD) in 2025, primarily for use in data centre processors.

In a bourse filing on Monday, IJM said its wholly owned subsidiary IJM Construction Sdn Bhd had accepted a letter of award for the design and construction of the facilities.

The project involves the construction of a four-storey production building, a three-storey central utility building and a single-storey wastewater treatment facility.

IJM said the 14-month project covers design development, procurement, construction, testing and commissioning, including civil and structural works, mechanical and electrical systems, cleanrooms, process utilities and supporting infrastructure.

The project will also incorporate Industrialised Building System (IBS) precast components, while the production building is targeted to achieve Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) Gold certification.

Construction is scheduled to commence in the fourth quarter of 2026, with completion expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

IJM group chief executive officer and managing director Datuk Lee Chun Fai said the contract award builds on the capabilities IJM Construction had developed in advanced manufacturing.

"Semiconductor facilities demand a high degree of technical coordination across the building, mechanical and engineering systems, cleanroom environment and process utilities, while meeting demanding programme requirements," he said in a separate statement.

"The scale and integrated scope of this project, together with its 14-month delivery programme, demonstrate our ability to manage technically complex projects at speed," Lee added.

The latest contract follows RM909.5 million worth of semiconductor and medical technology projects secured by IJM Construction in August 2026.

With the latest award, IJM Construction's outstanding order book stands at RM10.6 billion, covering building construction, advanced industrial facilities and civil engineering projects.

In June, AT&S announced plans to invest between €1.5 billion and €2 billion (approximately RM7 billion to RM9.3 billion) to expand its Kulim operations, backed by long-term commitments from AMD and another major technology customer.

The expansion includes fitting out its existing second plant and constructing a new manufacturing facility for IC substrate cores and advanced PCBs.

AT&S had initially committed €1.7 billion to the first phase of its Kulim campus, which was officially opened in January 2024, making it the largest single investment by an Austrian company in Malaysia at the time.

IJM shares closed at RM2.80 on Monday, down five sen or 1.75%, valuing the group at RM10.21 billion. Year-to-date the stock is up almost 26%

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): Steel manufacturer Malaysia Steel Works (KL) Bhd (KL:MASTEEL) on Monday announced the acquisition of a 51% stake in a high-voltage electrical engineering firm for RM12 million to expand into power infrastructure and data centre construction, as well as a proposed placement of nearly 4% of its issued share base to raise up to RM5.78 million for working capital.

The group said in a bourse filing that the acquisition of Anpec Global Corporation Sdn Bhd will allow it to tap into the latter's engineering capabilities and contracts with major utility companies, including Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) and Sabah Electricity Sdn Bhd.

Masteel has entered into a share sale agreement with Anpec founder and CEO Abd Rasid Mohamed Salleh for the acquisition. The purchase will be satisfied through RM3 million cash from internal funds, and the issuance of 45 million new Masteel shares at 20 sen apiece — a 7.93% premium to Masteel's five-day volume-weighted average market price (VWAMP) of 18.53 sen up to Oct 9.

This means Abd Rasid, who will retain a 49% interest in Anpec and continue overseeing its operations, will emerge as a substantial shareholder of Masteel with a 5.7% stake. This will be eventually diluted to 5.49% upon completion of the subsequent share placement.

Anpec specialises in high-voltage electrical infrastructure, substations and industrial electrical systems. It has an outstanding order book of RM107 million from six ongoing projects, with completion dates extending to 2028. It has also ventured into data centre-related power infrastructure, having completed a 275kV bulk electricity supply project for the Marmot Data Centre in Elmina West, Selangor, in December 2025.

The company is now bidding for roughly RM63 million worth of jobs involving TNB substations and high-voltage equipment testing services for Sabah Electricity.

Masteel executive vice-chairman Datuk Seri Tai Hean Leng said the acquisition would allow the group to combine its steel manufacturing operations with Anpec's expertise in power infrastructure engineering. The group is aiming to pursue opportunities arising from TNB's RM15 billion investment in the national electricity grid infrastructure, as highlighted under Budget 2027.

"We are positioned to execute larger green energy transition projects, providing green-certified steel alongside 132kV and 275kV substation engineering to connect large-scale solar facilities to the grid," he said in a statement.

The acquisition is targeted for completion by the end of 2026.

The subsequent share placement involves up to 29.48 million new shares, or 3.96% of its issued share base, to investors to be identified at an indicative price of 19.6 sen per share. The final price will be capped at a maximum discount of 10% to the five-day VMAMP before the price-fixing date.

Of the proceeds, RM5.53 million will be used for working capital, including utilities, staff costs and administrative expenses. The balance will be used to defray the proposal's expenses.

Together with the 45 million consideration shares to be issued for the Anpec acquisition, the group will be issuing up to 74.48 million new Masteel shares, equivalent to 10% of its existing issued share capital.

The group previously completed a private placement in August 2025, raising RM13.82 million from issuing 67.5 million new shares. Proceeds from that have since been fully utilised for working capital and related expenses.

Shares of Masteel, which manufactures steel billets, high-tensile deformed steel bars and mild steel round bars, rose 0.5 sen or 2.7% to close at 19 sen on Monday, valuing the company at RM141.9 million.

stories.title: Number of data center fires and power failures has doubled since 2024
stories.summary: New data from the Energy Incident Register reveals increasing faults
stories.title_zh: 自2024年以来数据中心火灾和电力故障数量翻倍
stories.content:
Data center fires and power failures have more than doubled since 2024, new incident data has revealed.

According to the Energy Incident Register, which provides an independently run public register of safety incidents in energy and grid infrastructure, the number of fires or power failures at data centers rose from just eight in 2024 to 20 in 2025 and 19 in 2026.

The Energy Incident Register now tracks data center incidents, based on public reporting, from 2010 to 2026 across 26 countries. Of 93 data center incidents in the period, 47 occurred in 2024 or later.

The US suffered the most from these incidents, with 33 incidents across the 16 year period – though this is to be expected given its market share. The UK saw the next highest incidence rate, with 14 incidents across the period.

Some 52 of the 93 incidents were fires or thermal events, with 18 classified as major.

The most common failures were in Uninterruptible Power Systems (UPS) and battery rooms, which represent 22 of the 93 incidents. Backup generators came next, with 15 incidents.

However, in the majority of incidents (53 of 93), no part was named in reporting.

*DCD* has reported on several major incidents at data centers this year, the latest being a fire at a data center in Gasan-dong, Seoul, South Korea, in September, and a fire in a Tata Communications center in India in June.

stories.title_zh: AI hyperscaler潜藏的巨大杠杆
stories.content:
While equity investors look to sunny futures, creditors are scrutinising liabilities like data centre leases

AT TIMES, creditors can feel like they are the only adults in the room. As artificial intelligence-driven exuberance drives stock markets higher, bond vigilantes are pushing Treasury rates higher, while credit markets are repricing data centre-related debt lower.

While equity analysts might get paid for dreamy earnings forecasts, the best creditors can hope for is repayment at par if a bond is held to maturity.

So they look at the details where, as ever, devils reside. For example, while the debt being taken on by hyperscalers to build out AI infrastructure is getting lots of attention and is even being blamed for crowding out Treasury bonds, creditors have taken this a step further in typically geeky fashion, scrutinising off-balance-sheet obligations such as leases.

stories.content:
(Oct 12): Tencent Holdings Ltd told fixed-income investors Monday that its planned bond offering of about US$5 billion (RM20.4 billion) will help finance AI-related capital expenditures, people familiar with the matter said, as it doubles down on the sector.

The Chinese technology and gaming giant could price the deal as early as Tuesday, it said in a call with the investors, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. The offering includes US$1.5 billion to US$2 billion across dollar tranches, and 20 billion yuan to 25 billion yuan from offshore yuan notes, the people said.

The proceeds will be primarily for general corporate purposes, such as AI-related capital expenditure, with the bulk of such spending directed toward chip purchases, the people added, citing Tencent’s management.

Both global and Chinese tech companies are increasingly turning to capital markets to fund costly AI investments, even as investors start to scrutinise whether spending on data centres, chips and model development will generate adequate returns.

SoftBank Group Corp recently raised US$11.1 billion through one of the largest corporate junk-bond offerings on record, while Alibaba Group Holding Ltd scooped up a record US$10.2 billion via a follow-on offering. Chinese AI model maker Z.AI Co garnered US$9.6 billion through its IPO, placements and convertible bonds.

Tencent said in the investor call that it currently has no plans to issue shares or convertible bonds, added the people, citing the company.

Tencent didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Tencent is also ramping up its AI-related spending amid a push to catch up to rivals such as ByteDance Ltd and Alibaba. The company hiked capital expenditures by 176% on AI projects and computing to 52.8 billion yuan in the June quarter, triggering a free-cash outflow of 13.8 billion yuan.

Tencent’s capital expenditure is likely to remain elevated through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027, suggesting annual spending of slightly more than 200 billion yuan based on second-quarter levels, the people said.

stories.title: Sponsored: Making every watt work
stories.summary: nVent’s David Wood explores how real-time power intelligence could be the key to unlocking stranded data center capacity and securing responsive AI infrastructure
stories.content:
Across the data center industry, the race to support AI is increasingly being measured in megawatts. As workloads become more demanding and compute densities continue to rise, operators are having to think carefully about how power is delivered and, crucially, how effectively it can be used.

While the conversation often starts at the facility level, the real challenge begins much closer to the rack.

For nVent, the rack itself is becoming a critical point of control. As AI workloads introduce rapid fluctuations in power demand, the ability to monitor and respond in real time will increasingly determine how effectively secured capacity can be utilized.

“The ceiling isn’t really about the silicon,” says David Wood, senior product manager of smart power at nVent. “It’s about power, and specifically, how intelligently you can deliver it.”

With more than 20 years of experience in the data center industry, Wood has witnessed the evolution of power infrastructure first-hand. Now, in a recent DCD>Broadcast episode, he shares why the next step will be about giving the rack the intelligence to respond to increasingly dynamic workloads.

## The rack-level power problem

Data center capacity is often discussed in terms of the overall power available to a facility. Operators may have 20, 50 or even more than 100MW at their disposal, but this doesn’t necessarily mean all this capacity can be put to work. As Wood explains:

“The constraint almost never shows up at this scale. It’s evident inside a single rack.”

At the rack level, provisioned power is either converted into useful compute or becomes stranded because something further downstream can’t respond quickly enough to the demands placed upon it.

Traditional enterprise workloads were relatively predictable, allowing infrastructure to be designed around stable patterns of consumption. AI workloads are an entirely different beast.

GPU clusters can rapidly move between idle and full power draw as workloads shift between training, inference, and communication cycles. Crucially, these changes can happen within milliseconds, creating a level of volatility that conventional infrastructure wasn’t designed to manage.

“This volatility is where the real damage happens,” says Wood. “Whether it’s thermal spikes, phase imbalances, or circuit breaker trips – when the power delivery can’t keep up, your own infrastructure becomes the bottleneck.”

This reality is driving a fundamental shift in power infrastructure. Rather than sizing systems to meet peak demand, operators increasingly need to manage power dynamically as workloads change.

## From monitoring to real-time intelligence

The problem with responding to these events effectively is that they can happen faster than traditional monitoring systems can detect them.

Conventional power distribution units (PDUs) typically rely on polling, where readings are requested at intervals of a second or more. This can provide a useful overview of consumption, but it risks missing the more transient events that matter most.

“If you’re polling every second or every few seconds, and you have a millisecond-scale swing, that reading is a snapshot of something that’s already over,” says Wood.

nVent’s approach is based on subsecond sampling and live streaming of power data. Beyond providing a record of what’s happened, the system is designed to provide visibility into how the workload is behaving as it happens.

“You can’t automate what you can’t see in real time,” adds Wood.

## The engine turning data into action

This is where nVent’s Intelligent PDU Platform with built-in event engine secures its place. Traditional metering can deliver accurate information about power consumption and quality, including billing-grade measurements, but this insight is still retrospective. The event engine is designed to take this information and put it into action to trigger an immediate response.

“The event engine can act on what’s happening right now because it runs on the PDU itself,” explains Wood.

The principle is relatively straightforward. An operator establishes a trigger, defines the condition under which it should be sustained, and then specifies the action that follows.

For example, a phase imbalance could be allowed to persist for a defined period before it exceeds a specified threshold and triggers an automated response. This helps prevent the system from reacting to momentary noise while ensuring it responds when it really matters.

## Beyond the PDU

For nVent, the longer-term opportunity lies in connecting power intelligence with the wider data center environment. Once the rack can understand its own power behavior and respond accordingly, this intelligence can be linked with other infrastructure systems, including critical cooling and workload management. This creates the possibility of coordinating systems around what the workload actually needs.

“We’re looking at it from the ground up at the rack level, to help secure better coordination across the entire facility,” says Wood.

nVent’s position is strengthened by its presence across both power and cooling. Rather than treating the two as entirely separate systems, the company is exploring how they can work together to anticipate workload requirements and respond accordingly.

On a broader level, rack-level intelligence can also feed into building management systems and data center infrastructure management software. What starts out as a local response can become part of a wider optimization strategy across the data hall.

This can help deliver more usable capacity from the same footprint, fewer nuisance trips, and closer coordination between power, cooling, and compute.

## The shift towards self-healing infrastructure

The ability to respond automatically is central to another concept Wood highlights: self-healing infrastructure. The term describes a move away from systems that simply identify a problem and notify an operator, towards more proactive infrastructure.

“Most of the infrastructure components and solutions that we use today, especially in power, tell you something went wrong,” says Wood. “What self-healing means is that the power distribution itself can do something about it before you even see the alert.”

Environmental monitoring provides another example. If sensors detect a temperature increase within a cabinet, predefined thresholds could trigger a response such as shutting down non-critical loads, reducing the heat being generated, and giving cooling systems time to react.

Inside high-density environments containing huge volumes of high-value equipment, the stakes are elevated. Consequently, for operators, the appeal of self-healing infrastructure is intrinsically tied to protecting valuable physical and computational investments.

## The bottom line

As rack densities continue to rise, however, intelligent power management will also need to evolve alongside the underlying architecture.

Wood points towards a future in which higher-voltage DC power is delivered directly at the rack, with architectures moving towards 400V and potentially 800V.

By reducing the number of power conversion stages between the source and the compute hardware, operators can potentially reduce losses while freeing up physical space to dedicate to compute.

“It’s a real architectural shift, and it doesn’t happen overnight,” says Wood. “But it’s coming, and rack intelligence has to move with it.”

Ultimately, the argument for intelligent power comes down to the fundamental reality that secured capacity is only valuable if it can actually be deployed effectively.

“The risk has never really been about running out of power. It’s about stranding the power you already have and not making use of it because the rack can’t act fast enough,” he continues.

This makes the rack an increasingly important part of data center power strategies. With real-time visibility, automated responses, and close integration between cooling and workload management, power distribution can become an active participant in infrastructure optimization.

For Wood, the ultimate goal is to ensure that the enormous investments being made in AI infrastructure deliver as much useful compute as possible.

“We invest a lot of money in our data centers today, and it’s really important to be able to make the most of it,” he concludes. “nVent is here to help extract the greatest value out of that investment and to be responsible in our environmental approaches by utilizing our resources most efficiently.”

KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): Kinergy Advancement Bhd (KL:KINERGY) has secured a RM47.5 million subcontract from Gamuda Bhd's (KL:GAMUDA) unit for electrical works at a hyperscale data centre in Bandar Spring Hill, Port Dickson.

The subcontract was awarded by Gamuda Bhd’s wholly-owned subsidiary, Gamuda Engineering Sdn Bhd, for the data centre for a multi-national technology company headquartered in the US. The company was not named in the filing on Monday (Oct 12).

Under the contract, Kinergy will design, supply, install, test and commission the electrical infrastructure, including substations, transformers, power distribution systems, cabling, lighting, backup power systems and EV charging facilities.

The works are scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2028.

Kinergy’s executive deputy chairman and group managing director Datuk Dr Lai Keng Onn said the award signals the group’s growing recognition in the data centre sector and its technical capabilities in high-specification infrastructure.

Lai cited Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) figures that showed RM95.8 billion worth of data centre and cloud-computing investments being approved in Malaysia in the first half of 2026.

“As development grows in scale and complexity, we see increasing demand for specialised engineering and power infrastructure, creating a strong opportunity for Kinergy to deepen its participation in the sector,” Lad added.

Kinergy’s share price was unchanged at 39.5 sen during Monday’s mid-day break, valuing it at RM852.31 million.

stories.title: Submer India, BSNL Tower Corporation to develop AI-ready data centres across India
stories.summary: Submer India Private Limited and BSNL Tower Corporation Limited (BTCL) signed an MoU at India Mobile Congress 2026. The collaboration will explore sovereign, AI-ready data centre infrastructure across India.
stories.content:
NEW DELHI: Submer India and BSNL Tower Corporation Limited (BTCL) on Monday said they have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) at the recently concluded India Mobile Congress (IMC 2026) to explore the development of sovereign, AI-ready data centre infrastructure across India.The collaboration will focus on infrastructure designed for artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) requirements. Submer and BTCL will jointly assess opportunities for GPU-as-a-Service, sovereign AI cloud infrastructure, and edge and micro-edge data centres.They will also evaluate large-scale data centre projects up to 20 MW. The parties will assess the suitability of BSNL premises and data centre facilities for transformation into distributed edge infrastructure.These assessments will consider technical and commercial feasibility, connectivity, scalability, and energy efficiency. They will also address the requirements of government, public sector undertakings (PSU), enterprise, research, and institutional workloads.“AI will play an increasingly important role in India’s digital transformation, creating demand for secure, high-performance computing infrastructure that can serve the country at scale,” said Robert J Ravi, CMD, BSNL. “This MoU marks an important step in evaluating how BSNL’s nationwide infrastructure and connectivity footprint can support sovereign AI capabilities. Our collaboration with Submer will help us explore an infrastructure model designed around India’s long-term digital priorities.”“Government bodies and enterprises need a practical path to adopt AI without compromising performance, security, or data sovereignty,” said Sudhakar Rao Papa, director (enterprise business), BSNL. “By assessing GPU-as-a-Service, sovereign cloud and distributed edge infrastructure, this collaboration aims to bring AI computing capacity closer to organizations across India and support a broader range of public-sector and enterprise applications.”“India has the talent, demand, and digital reach to become a global AI infrastructure leader. The next step is to build the physical capacity that turns that ambition into deployable compute,” said Anupam Shrivastava, Submer India Head. “Together with BTCL, we are bringing infrastructure, network reach, and engineering expertise into one model. Our goal is clear: make sovereign AI capacity available where it is needed, from strategic edge locations to large-scale AI data centers.”Under the pact, Submer will apply its expertise in integrated data centre architecture, liquid cooling, and high-density computing. BTCL will coordinate access to relevant BSNL premises and data centre facilities for feasibility studies.A key assessment area will be a sovereign AI cloud model. This model will leverage BSNL’s network footprint and indigenous 4G and 5G core to support scalable, low-latency GPU-as-a-Service. The collaboration also includes coordinated opportunity development and technical workshops.

stories.content:
This will be one of the largest deals for the sector in Asia

\[HONG KONG\] Bain Capital-owned Bridge Data Centres is in talks with banks to more than double the size of an existing loan to about US$6.6 billion, people familiar with the matter said, in what would be one of the largest deals for the sector in Asia.

The move is an extension of a previous effort to increase the size to at least US$5 billion from an original US$2.8 billion that it obtained last year for its operations in Malaysia.

The expanded deal could be launched into the market as early as November, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussion private matters.

At the same time, plans for a loan of up to US$6 billion for a Thailand-based data centre have stalled, the people said, around the time the South-east Asian nation decided last month to suspend the construction of 49 data centres amid concerns over energy usage.

A spokesperson for Bridge said “as a matter of policy, we do not comment on unverified information or market speculation”.

Data centre operators have been rushing to take on additional debt as they seek to expand amid growing demand spurred by the AI boom. Moody’s Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion to flow into data centre-related investments over the next five years, with much of the spending financed through debt.

Still, signs are emerging that global investors are starting to push back when they perceive valuations to be frothy. Banks are increasingly mindful of their exposure to the sector as they bump-up against lending limits.

The most salient recent example of investor hesitation came just last week when Firmus Grid pulled an attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings after running into difficulties convincing some potential investors of its steep increase in market value.

Wall Street has grown increasingly anxious about AI and its potential to impact other businesses, a fear that spurred investors to dump a range of stocks from Expedia to Salesforce earlier this year.

BDC is a unit of Wintrix, formerly known as Chindata Group, the Chinese data centre operator that Bain Capital took private in 2023 in a deal worth about US$3.2 billion. The firm currently has facilities in Malaysia, Thailand, and India, according to its company website. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: India's semiconductor sector sees M&A, investment surge for AI data centers
stories.summary: India's semiconductor ecosystem is experiencing significant growth in mergers, acquisitions, and investments. This expansion is driven by government support, a strong talent pool, and increasing global interest, particularly for AI data centre applications.
stories.content:
India's semiconductor sector is witnessing a surge in mergers, acquisitions, and investments, driven by both international chipmakers and domestic companies. This growth reflects a maturing ecosystem and rising investor confidence, with implications for AI data centre applications.Seven acquisitions were announced in 2026, reflecting interest in India’s semiconductor capabilities. Five-year data from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Tracxn, and industry estimates signal this maturing ecosystem. The ₹76,000-crore India Semiconductor Mission in 2021 sparked immediate interest, drawing $25.1 million to local startups that year. Momentum surged alongside key milestones, such as Micron’s chip packaging plant in Sanand, Gujarat.Startups raised $153.7 million in 2023, $113.7 million in 2024, and $474 million in 2025. They added another $228.7 million through early October this year. The number of first-time investors in the semiconductor industry followed a similar trajectory, jumping from 12 in 2021 to 80 in 2024. The Union Cabinet approved the Tata Group’s first chip fabrication unit in Dholera, Gujarat, in 2024.In 2023, Indian semiconductor startups saw $14.4 million in seed-stage investment, $31.3 million in early-stage, and $108 million in late-stage investment. Two years later, in 2025, seed-stage investments rose to $33.4 million, and early-stage investment grew to $79.4 million. Late-stage investment in Indian semiconductor startups more than tripled to $361 million in 2025.Rajan Anandan, managing director of global venture capital firm Peak XV Partners, said India is seeing the beginning of a massive semiconductor startup ecosystem. He noted that talent is the core reason, as 20 per cent of global semiconductor designers are in India. Peak XV has invested in semiconductor startups Agrani Labs, C2i Semiconductors, InCore Semiconductors, and Mindgrove.
### M&A activity and AI data centre focus

A similar trend is emerging in mergers and acquisitions. Among 3,557 companies in the semiconductor and allied sectors, 68 were acquired at a median price of $33.7 million. As many as 27 M&A deals were announced over the last five years, including seven in 2026 alone. The median deal price jumped to $125 million in these deals.One of the largest acquisitions in the last five years was Narayan Powertech, a Vadodara-based manufacturer. In 2024, New Hampshire–headquartered Standex acquired the company for $261.9 million. Japan’s Renesas bought Bengaluru-headquartered Steradian Semiconductors for nearly $36 million in 2022. Steradian provides radar solutions for object recognition.Germany’s Infineon in August 2026 announced the acquisition of Bengaluru-based C2i Semiconductors. C2i specialises in software-defined multiphase controllers and smart power stages for AI data centre applications. Adam White, president of Infineon’s Power Systems division, said this acquisition strengthens Infineon’s leadership in power solutions for AI data centres. He added that it creates a new centre of excellence for digital power technologies in India.M&A activity over the past five years is not restricted to pure-play chip designers. It now extends into companies focused on water recycling and power optimisation for silicon chips, experts noted. Sateesh Andra, managing partner at venture capital firm Endiya Partners, said there is a gradual shift towards intellectual property ownership. Indian startups are moving beyond design services to develop proprietary semiconductor products and technologies.Government support for semiconductor initiatives and manufacturing incentives is improving ecosystem infrastructure and investment visibility, Andra said. More engineers with global semiconductor experience are now launching deep-tech ventures.

India's data centre sector saw a return to multi-city investment strategies in the first half of 2026, according to a recent market research report. Investors committed over 85 per cent of $38 billion in H1 2026 to new projects spread across multiple hubs, CBRE's report stated.This follows a period dominated by single-site mega projects, with multi-city capital deployment now accounting for the majority. Large capacity additions are typically spread across several cities to build resilience.Between 2021 and 2023, multi-city portfolios represented over 60 per cent of total investments. This included targeted spending in primary hubs such as Mumbai, Delhi-NCR, Bengaluru, and Chennai.The trend temporarily shifted in 2024 and 2025, with Hyderabad capturing 23 per cent and 15 per cent of total investments respectively. Tier-II cities secured 16 per cent and 27 per cent in those years, driven by standalone mega projects like Google’s centre in Vizag.India added 130 megawatts (MW) of new capacity in H1 2026. Mumbai accounted for 94 per cent of this new supply, while Chennai contributed the remaining 6 per cent.Established micro markets like Navi Mumbai and Chennai’s Siruseri continue to see significant activity. Mumbai currently holds over 52 per cent of the country’s total data centre capacity, with Chennai at 18 per cent.More than 200 MW is expected to be added in the second half of the year. This puts India’s total operational capacity on track to reach 2 gigawatts (GW) by the end of 2026.While over 80 per cent of India’s operational capacity remains concentrated in Mumbai, Chennai, and Delhi-NCR, incremental capacity is expected in secondary and emerging hubs. This is driven by better availability of land, power, and water.Anshuman Magazine, chairperson and CEO (India, SEA, Middle East and Africa) of CBRE, told TOI that India’s data centre landscape is becoming more geographically diverse. He added that Hyderabad is emerging as a key growth market.Operators are expected to add more capacity in Bengaluru, Kolkata, and Visakhapatnam, Magazine said. They weigh access to land, power, water, and connectivity, he noted.Magazine clarified that the lower share of new supply in H1 2026 does not indicate a move away from Chennai by hyperscalers. It reflects a maturing multi-hub market, he stated.Recent investments bring India’s total data centre commitments to around $173 billion since 2021. Over 15 per cent of this capital is specifically dedicated to supporting Artificial Intelligence (AI).Large global tech companies and cloud providers, known as hyperscalers, continue to drive most of the real estate demand. ReNew Wind Energy Pvt Ltd, a wholly-owned subsidiary of clean energy company ReNew, has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the government of the western Indian state of Maharashtra for a proposed ₹70,000 crore (US$ 7.3 billion) integrated green data center park in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR).

The green data center park project aligns with Maharashtra’s goal to become a US$ 1 trillion economy by 2030. Readers would recall that just this year, Maharashtra has entered into several MoUs and agreements with different digital infrastructure providers for projects in the wider MMR and especially in areas in and around Navi Mumbai. These include projects by Tillman Global Holdings, AirtTrunk, Tata Group, and most recently, Trentrar.

According to a report by Business Standard, the planned capacity for the project stands at 750 MW. The green data center part will be developed near Mumbai in the region’s emerging data center corridor spread across Panvel, Khalapur, Taloja and Bhokharpada.

“A defining feature of the proposed park is its focus on green power for data centre operations,” ReNew said in a statement to Business Standard. “The Integrated Green Data Center Park would be required to use 51 percent green power for maintaining its operations. The project is also envisaged with dedicated power infrastructure, including facilitation for two incoming feeders from independent sources to the data centre park substation.” The company says that the project is expected to begin operations in 2028.

The MoU was signed by ReNew’s state head, and P.Anbalagan who serves as Principal Secretary, Industries, Investment & Services Department, and CEO, Invest Maharashtra. The agreement outlines how the state government will facilitate obtaining necessary permissions, registrations, approvals, clearances etc. and offer fiscal incentives as per relevant policies and regulations.

stories.summary: New Zealand fibre network operator EonFibre has launched Zone Direct, a connectivity service aimed at data centre developers, hyperscalers, neocloud providers and carriers considering entering or expanding in the country. The service is designed to help investors assess connectivity during site selection, covering connections to existing and proposed data centres, cable landing stations and international […]
stories.content:
New Zealand fibre network operator EonFibre has launched Zone Direct, a connectivity service aimed at data centre developers, hyperscalers, neocloud providers and carriers considering entering or expanding in the country. The service is designed to help investors assess connectivity during site selection, covering connections to existing and proposed data centres, cable landing stations and international capacity.

Zone Direct is based around six data centre zones identified by Invest New Zealand in its Data and Digital Infrastructure sector overview: North Waikato, Taupō, Taranaki, Manawatū, South Canterbury and Central Otago.

The zones were selected for their access to high-voltage electricity infrastructure, backhaul fibre and potential speed to power. Invest New Zealand says some sites within the zones could have infrastructure connections for new data centres within one to three years. However, a footnote to the report’s zone map cautions that the listed capacities cannot all be achieved simultaneously because of constraints on total system capacity.

EonFibre chief executive Richard Mooney said connectivity needed to be considered alongside power availability and land when investors assessed potential locations. “The case for data centres in New Zealand starts with renewable power, land and stability,” Mooney said.

“Investors also need to know how capacity at a new campus will reach customers in Australia, Asia and the United States. National and international bandwidth is our core business. We want to be part of those conversations early, while sites are still being chosen, to enable efficiencies across the development and operational process.”

Zone Direct will provide a connectivity brief for each zone, outlining route options, physical diversity and indicative latency to international cable landing stations and destinations in Australia and the US. The service will also offer site-specific desktop assessments, a single point of contact for network planning and delivery, and the design, construction, operation and maintenance of campus connectivity networks.

EonFibre operates more than 11,000km of fibre between Whangārei in the north and Invercargill in the south. Its network includes metropolitan fibre rings in Auckland, Hamilton, Wellington and Christchurch, three diverse routes between the North and South Islands, and the Aqualink domestic submarine cable.

The operator says its network reaches major data centres and exchange sites across New Zealand, including the Auckland clusters at Albany, Westgate, the CBD and Silverdale.

Internationally, EonFibre co-owns the Tasman Global Access cable between New Zealand and Sydney and provides capacity on the Hawaiki and Southern Cross systems. It also has points of presence in Australia and the US, alongside partnerships with global operators for onward connectivity.

EonFibre has also worked with Google on fibre infrastructure for the Honomoana submarine cable, which landed north of Auckland. The cable adds international capacity and connectivity between New Zealand, Australia and other Pacific destinations.

Zone Direct combines these national and international network assets with EonFibre’s existing Direct Fibre, FlexWave managed wavelength services of up to 400Gbps, data centre interconnection and international capacity.

“Developers want to know how many physically separate routes reach a site, how far it is to the international cables, and how quickly capacity can be delivered,” Mooney said. “Because we hold both the national routes and the international capacity, we can answer those questions and deliver the service end to end, from the campus to Sydney or the United States.”

### New Zealand targets data centre investment

**Invest New Zealand’s sector overview** positions the country as a potential location for data centre and AI infrastructure investment, citing renewable electricity, available land, a cool climate, political stability and international connectivity.

The report says hydropower accounted for 54% of New Zealand’s electricity generation in 2025, while geothermal contributed 20%. It also points to further renewable generation development as an opportunity to support additional data centre demand.

New Zealand’s electricity system is connected through a national high-voltage transmission network operated by Transpower. The report says data centres accounted for approximately 0.6% of grid electricity consumption in 2025, while planned transmission upgrades and new generation projects are intended to support future demand.

Connectivity is another part of the country’s investment proposition. The report identifies four operational international submarine cable systems serving New Zealand: the Southern Cross Cable Network, Southern Cross NEXT, Hawaiki and Tasman Global Access. It also highlights Honomoana, which landed in 2026, and several proposed systems intended to expand international capacity and route diversity.

The report, citing BCG analysis, forecasts that New Zealand’s data centre capacity could grow from approximately 125MW in 2025 to 425MW by 2035 based on domestic demand. Export-oriented development could raise total capacity to around 725MW in its base scenario or as much as 1,425MW in a high-growth scenario.

The six zones form part of the government’s effort to direct investors towards locations where electricity infrastructure and fibre routes could support new development. EonFibre’s new service is intended to give prospective developers a clearer view of connectivity options before they commit to a site.

The event will provide an opportunity to hear from industry participants and discuss the country’s evolving cloud and data centre landscape.*

EonFibre has launched Zone Direct for data centre developers and network operators planning to enter or expand in New Zealand. The product targets projects in six data centre zones identified by Invest New Zealand.

The offer provides a connectivity brief for each zone, including route options, physical diversity and indicative latency to New Zealand's international cable landing stations, Australia and the United States. It also includes site connectivity assessments during site selection, a single point of contact from early assessment through network planning and delivery, and the design, build, operation and maintenance of campus connectivity networks.

Richard Mooney, Chief Executive Officer of EonFibre, said the company wants to engage with investors while projects are still at an early stage.

"The case for data centres in New Zealand starts with renewable power, land and stability," Mooney said. "Investors also need to know how capacity at a new campus will reach customers in Australia, Asia and the United States. National and international bandwidth is our core business. We want to be part of those conversations early, while sites are still being chosen, to create efficiencies across development and operations."

The company has also worked with Google on fibre infrastructure linked to the Honomoana cable, which lands north of Auckland.

### Site questions

The new offer is built around practical issues data centre developers assess before committing to a site. These include the number of physically separate fibre routes available, the distance to international cable systems and the likely time needed to deliver bandwidth to a new campus.

"Developers want to know how many physically separate routes reach a site, how far it is to the international cables, and how quickly capacity can be delivered," Mooney said. "Because we hold both the national routes and the international capacity, we can answer those questions and deliver the service end to end, from the campus to Sydney or the United States."

Zone Direct draws on EonFibre's existing services, including Direct Fibre, FlexWave managed wavelengths of up to 400 Gbit/s, data centre interconnection and international capacity. EonFibre works directly with developers, hyperscalers, carriers and data centre operators, with commercial terms tailored to long-term infrastructure projects.

stories.title: Architecting digital trust for Malaysia's sovereign AI future
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence is moving into the systems that power banking, public services, industry and critical infrastructure. But having the computing power to run AI is only part of the story. Malaysia also needs to secure its data, test how AI systems perform and know whether their outputs can be trusted.

stories.title_zh: 为马来西亚主权AI未来构建数字信任架构
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence is moving into the systems that power banking, public services, industry and critical infrastructure. But having the computing power to run AI is only part of the story. Malaysia also needs to secure its data, test how AI systems perform and know whether their outputs can be trusted.

This is the role MIMOS Berhad is looking to play as Malaysia builds its own sovereign AI capabilities, with Group Chief Technology Officer Dr Zulaikha Kadim working across areas including deepfake detection, AI-driven cybersecurity, trusted digital identity and cognitive AI.

As AI takes on bigger, higher-stakes roles, it can no longer be judged simply by how fast or intelligent it is, she says. Its outputs must also be accurate, secure, explainable and accountable.

“AI is no longer used only to generate text or images. It is increasingly being embedded into systems that influence decisions in public services, industry, finance and critical infrastructure,” she points out.

In other words, AI now has to be checked and proven, not just made faster or smarter. That is the idea behind Digital Trust: being able to rely on what a digital system tells you, whether a transaction is genuine, a person is who they claim to be, or a record has not been changed.

MIMOS is developing these digital trust capabilities through its Trusted Intelligence Platform, as part of its efforts to turn national priorities into technologies that can be tested locally. The two concepts are closely linked, but Zulaikha says they serve different purposes.

“Digital Trust is the confidence that people and organisations have in a digital system, transaction or AI-supported decision. They need to know that the system is secure, that the information has not been altered and that the identity or content involved is genuine,” she explains.

That work is aligned with Malaysia’s broader push to build trusted and sovereign AI capabilities, with MIMOS translating national priorities into technologies that can be developed and tested locally.

Under the 13th Malaysia Plan (RMK13), MIMOS is developing blockchain-secured trusted logs, deepfake detection and AI-driven cybersecurity, as well as Mi-Muallim, which detects deviations in verified content. The work also extends to cognitive AI for vision and robotics.

Deepfakes are one area where the technology is being put to the test. MIMOS is developing detection tools while studying how synthetic and manipulated content is created, allowing researchers to understand how quickly the technology behind such manipulation is evolving.

“MIMOS is addressing deepfakes from both the defensive and research perspectives. Under RMK13, we are developing AI-based detection technologies to assess multimedia integrity, while researching generative AI to understand how synthetic and manipulated content is created,” says Zulaikha.

But detection alone is not enough. She says the technology also has to work in Malaysia, where language, accents and demographics can differ from the data used to train overseas models.

“Localisation is equally important. Detection models developed overseas may not perform consistently with Bahasa Melayu, mixed-language conversations, Malaysian accents or our diverse population,” she adds.

This means building local datasets and testing methods to give organisations evidence they can use in investigations, risk assessments and operational decisions. From there, MIMOS takes the technology into controlled proof-of-concept projects with users, testing how it performs in real operating environments before wider deployment.

“Their feedback also allows us to refine the technology around genuine requirements rather than assumptions made by researchers. Therefore, the objective is not to conduct a showcase for its own sake. It is to generate evidence, confirm the value proposition and create a credible pathway towards adoption and commercialisation,” says Zulaikha.

That approach also shapes how MIMOS works alongside global technology providers as Malaysia expands its cloud, data centre and computing capacity. Sovereignty does not mean shutting out global technology, but retaining control over sensitive data and critical AI capabilities, she says.

“Global technology providers give Malaysia access to advanced cloud infrastructure, computing platforms, foundational AI models and global innovation networks. We should benefit from their speed, scale and investment. However, Malaysia must retain the ability to protect sensitive data, verify how an AI system performs in our environment and decide which workloads should remain local or on-premises,” she adds.

MIMOS therefore takes a hybrid approach to computing, combining its own on-premises graphics processing units with secure cloud resources and infrastructure from strategic partners. Sensitive workloads can remain in controlled local environments, while larger workloads can use external infrastructure where appropriate.

“The important point is that sovereignty is not determined only by who owns the hardware. It also depends on whether Malaysia retains control over its data, models, security requirements and critical AI capabilities,” she says.

The longer-term opportunity is to turn those capabilities into platforms, standards and assurance services that can be deployed beyond individual projects.

“If we can convert these capabilities into repeatable platforms, standards and assurance services, Malaysia can support both domestic adoption and regional deployment. The opportunity is larger than becoming a user or host of AI infrastructure,” says Zulaikha.

“Malaysia can become a regional location where high-impact AI and digital content are independently tested, validated and trusted. That is where technological sovereignty can translate into economic value.”

For more on MIMOS’ applied research and development work, visit mimos.my.

stories.content:
Walk into many legacy data halls and you’ll find the same thing: racks breathing air colder than the hardware needs, cooled by equipment sized for a load that changed a decade ago. For years, that waste stayed an internal line item. A growing number of building performance, emissions and data-reporting requirements in the US and Europe are bringing that inefficiency under greater regulatory scrutiny.

That shift turns efficiency in existing facilities from a good intention into an obligation with a deadline. It also puts the focus on the part of the industry with the most room for improvement: portfolios of enterprise data centers, network facilities and Edge sites that were built for different workloads and have been expanded piece by piece ever since.

## Efficiency is becoming a reporting obligation

Building performance policy has moved well past a handful of early-adopter cities. More than 50 US states and cities now have benchmarking or performance requirements for large buildings on the books.

Colorado is a useful example of where these programs are headed. Its statewide program covers buildings of 50,000 square feet or more, and starting in 2030, HB25-1269 allows fines of up to $2,300 for every 30 days a covered building remains out of compliance with applicable performance standards, with higher penalties possible for subsequent violations.

Data centers in the program are measured against Power Usage Effectiveness targets. Operators can request a target tailored to their facility, but only with a detailed engineering audit to back it up. The flexibility goes to the operators who already have the data. New York City’s Local Law 97 assesses $268 for every metric ton of CO2 equivalent a covered building emits over its limit, and those limits tighten in 2030.

In Europe, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 requires every data center with at least 500 kW of installed IT power demand to report 24 key performance indicators spanning energy, ICT and data traffic to a European database each year.

Operators are responding unevenly. Uptime Institute’s 2026 Global Data Center Survey found that the share of organizations actively collecting sustainability metrics has returned to a gradual upward trend, while carbon emissions tracking remains a minority activity. For facilities subject to these rules, incomplete operating data can become a compliance risk.

## Legacy infrastructure holds the biggest efficiency gain**s**

Demand growth raises the stakes. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates US data centers consumed 192 TWh in 2024, about 4.7 percent of national electricity, and projects that share could reach 11.8 percent by 2030 in its reference case.

New, highly efficient AI capacity will carry much of this growth, yet the same Uptime survey found legacy infrastructure is slowing global efficiency progress, with average PUE improving only slightly this year.

Existing sites are where regulatory exposure and improvement potentially overlap, and where operators often have the least visibility. A portfolio assembled over 15 or 20 years typically runs several building management systems, cooling plants of different ages and set points chosen conservatively long ago and never revisited.

## Retrofits that pay for themselves

The measures that recover efficiency in these facilities are well understood, and few of them require replacing major cooling equipment such as chillers, CRAC units or air handlers:

- Full-aisle containment, plus sealing of cable cutouts, floor gaps and missing blanking panels, so supply and return air stop mixing.
- Plenum repair to restore the underfloor static pressure that raised-floor cooling depends on.
- EC fan retrofits with dynamic controls, so fans track real thermal load instead of running at a fixed worst-case speed.
- Filter optimization to maintain required particulate protection while reducing unnecessary airflow resistance.
- Temperature set point optimization within the ASHRAE-recommended envelope of 18°C to 27°C (64.4°F to 80.6°F) for air-cooled IT equipment.

The last item is the most frequently overlooked. Many legacy rooms still deliver inlet air below the bottom of ASHRAE’s recommended range, wasting cooling energy the hardware doesn't need.

ENERGY STAR estimates data centers can save four to five percent in energy costs for every 1°F increase in server inlet temperature. Containment and airflow repairs are what make it safe to raise set points without creating hot spots.

## Measure first, then verify every step

The order of operations determines whether these retrofits produce measurable, defensible results. The sequence that holds up is to establish a measured baseline with rack-level thermal and energy monitoring, make one category of change at a time and verify the result before moving to the next.

Documenting each step this way does three jobs. It confirms each intervention reduced thermal risk instead of adding it, it supports measurement and verification for utility incentive programs and it creates the auditable data trail that performance standards and disclosure rules require.

A recent Promera customer proof of concept at a national media and connectivity provider shows how this approach can work in practice. The operator runs six national data centers and roughly 600 local market sites, and cited state building performance legislation, alongside a corporate carbon-neutrality goal, as the reason to manage thermal load more dynamically. The team baselined a pilot site with real-time monitoring software, then layered in containment, filter changes and EC fan retrofits while tracking the effect of each.

Results to date include more than $50,000 in estimated cooling energy savings at an electricity price of roughly seven cents per kWh, a 1.79-year payback on the energy savings portion of the project and a potential 56 percent return on that segment.

Average rack temperatures rose a safe 7.2°F, and the number of racks running below 64.4°F, the floor of ASHRAE’s recommended range, fell by 31.5 percent. The same monitoring data now feeds the operator’s internal sustainability reporting and state compliance reporting, and it documented the project for a utility rebate.

## Treat 2030 as a budget deadline

The low power price in that example matters. A retrofit that pays for itself in under two years at seven cents per kWh pays off even faster where electricity costs more. Add the fines an operator avoids by meeting its performance targets, and the payback period shrinks again.

With 2030 only three or four budget cycles away, operators should begin establishing baselines and sequencing improvements now. Organizations that act early can plan retrofits across their portfolios, pursue available incentives and enter mandatory compliance periods with years of verified performance data. Those that wait may face the same work on a tighter timeline, with less evidence to demonstrate progress.

stories.title: Hyperscale Data plans Patriot BTC subsidiary for Bitcoin mining business
stories.summary: Will transfer Montana data center to new company
stories.content:
Hyperscale Data plans to form a new subsidiary, Patriot BTC, to hold its Bitcoin mining operations as it develops its Michigan data center for AI workloads.

Under the proposal announced on September 22, the company would transfer its Montana data center, Bitcoin miners, mining equipment, and associated infrastructure to the subsidiary.

“Bitcoin mining and AI data center development have different capital requirements, operating priorities and value drivers,” explained Milton 'Todd' Ault III, Hyperscale Data’s executive chairman.

The firm is evaluating ways to position Patriot BTC within a publicly traded entity, potentially through a separation or another transaction. At the time of the announcement, the subsidiary had not been formed and no transaction structure or separation had been approved. Any transaction would require board approval and compliance with applicable legal and regulatory requirements.

The proposed restructuring follows Hyperscale Data’s shutdown of Bitcoin mining at its Dowagiac, Michigan, facility on September 1, as it prepares the site for a California-based neocloud customer.

Its Alliance Cloud Services subsidiary announced a master services agreement with the customer in June, covering an initial 20MW of critical AI compute capacity. The agreement has a ten-year term and two five-year extension options. Hyperscale Data expects revenue above $1.2bn if both term extensions are exercised.

According to the company’s SEC filing, the customer also has a right of first offer for an additional 32MW of critical AI compute capacity, subject to availability.

In a September 17 update, Hyperscale Data said it was targeting the start of operations under the agreement in November 2026 and had invested more than $70m in Alliance Cloud Services and the Michigan facility.

The company reiterated on October 5 that the campus could ultimately support more than 300MW of total power capacity. Expansion beyond the initial 20MW remains subject to financing, utility agreements, engineering, regulatory approvals and other conditions.

stories.title_zh: NVIDIA考虑通过投资或算力交易加深与开源模型开发商Reflection AI的合作
stories.content:
Reflection has also struck billion-dollar deals with SpaceX and cloud provider Nebius Group

NVIDIA is in talks to boost its investment in Reflection AI or offer the US startup computing power, a move that would strengthen ties with a key developer of open-weight models, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The discussions are at an early stage, and no terms have been reached, said the person, who asked not to be identified because the matter is private. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while Reflection declined to comment.

The *Financial Times* previously reported on the talks, saying they could potentially lead to an acquisition offer. Possible deal structures include an “acqui-hire,” in which Nvidia would hire staff and license technology; an agreement to provide the startup with more chips; or an increase in Nvidia’s equity investment, the newspaper said.

The startup debuted its first open-weight model, Beam, earlier in October, pushing into a market where Chinese startups have a strong presence. With such software, developers release the model’s parameters, or weights, allowing others to freely use and modify the technology.

Beam is designed to perform well for business customers and developers on coding and AI agent tasks while costing less than many competitors’ products, Reflection said on Monday (Oct 5). It said Beam scores comparably on advanced reasoning benchmarks to GLM-5.2, a flagship open model from China’s Z.AI.

The startup, which was founded by two former Google DeepMind researchers, has held talks to raise US$2.5 billion at a valuation of US$25 billion, the *Wall Street Journal* previously reported.

Reflection has also struck billion-dollar deals with Elon Musk’s SpaceX and cloud provider Nebius Group to secure computing power to develop its models.

A Reflection tie-up would add to a frenzy of transactions by Nvidia in recent months. The chipmaker, which is the world’s most valuable company, has used its financial might to cultivate the broader AI industry.

The deals have included a US$13 billion agreement to buy AI model company Hugging Face in September and a roughly US$20 billion licensing pact with the chip startup Groq.

Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang is also a major proponent of open-weight models.

The hope is that US development of the technology could curb startups’ use of Chinese open-weight models, which are much cheaper to use than ones from American companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, while not far behind in intelligence.

The US government is also encouraging the development of such models.

“We need to ensure America has leading open models founded on American values,” reads US President Donald Trump’s July 2025 AI action plan. “Open-source and open-weight models could become global standards in some areas of business and in academic research worldwide.” BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Drax data centre campus faces scrutiny over biomass emissions
stories.summary: Drax's plans for a major data centre campus at its Selby power station are under scrutiny for potential biomass demand and emissions. Campaigners estimate that supplying the proposed behind-the-meter capacity could require 4.9 million tonnes of wood annually, producing 8.6 million tonnes of CO2 emissions.
stories.content:
Drax's plans for a major data centre campus at its Selby power station are under scrutiny over potential biomass demand and emissions. Campaigners estimate that supplying the proposed behind-the-meter capacity with biomass could require around 4.9 million tonnes of wood annually.The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) estimates this scenario could produce 8.6 million tonnes of CO2 emissions annually. This figure is nearly twice the yearly emissions from Gatwick flights.Drax initially outlined plans for an approximately 100MW data centre at Selby power station in December 2025. This first phase would use electricity imported through the grid.The company has also explored a larger 1.2GW-scale campus, which could include behind-the-meter electricity from its generation assets. The NRDC stress-tested 1.1GW of this potential capacity.Drax disputes the NRDC's methodology and assumptions about how the larger campus would be powered. This dispute adds uncertainty to the company's data centre plans.Further uncertainty arose when The Times reported that the proposal to designate Drax Power Station as an AI Growth Zone was rejected by the Government. North Yorkshire Council no longer supports this designation.AI Growth Zone status could have addressed power, planning, and investment barriers for the expansion. York and North Yorkshire is not among the five zones currently designated by the Government.While Drax disputes the NRDC's figures, the group's 4.9 million tonne biomass estimate broadly matches an extrapolation from Drax's own 2025 data. Drax reported consuming 7.74 million tonnes of biomass at its power station in 2025.Its generation figures indicated around 15.36TWh of biomass electricity during that year. Applying this fuel intensity to a constant 1.1GW load implies an annual biomass requirement of approximately 4.85 million tonnes.Drax states it has not committed to continuously supplying the entire data centre campus from its biomass units. Its Low-Carbon Dispatchable Contract for Difference requires Government permission to supply a data centre directly from its biomass units during its term.

stories.title: Cipher extends Barber Lake data center lease commitments to 20 years
stories.summary: Fluidstack and unnamed AI lab agree lengthy leases
stories.content:
AI data center company Cipher Digital has agreed deals with Fluidstack and an unnamed AI lab to lease space at the firm's Barber Lake data center campus in Colorado City, Texas, for the next 20 years.

The agreements, announced on September 25, amend AI cloud provider Fluidstack’s existing lease and secure a binding commitment from an unnamed AI lab to enter into a separate ten-year lease once Fluidstack’s term ends.

Cipher expects the additional commitment to generate around $5.2bn, raising total contracted revenue at Barber Lake from $3.8bn to more than $9bn, according to the announcement. The second lease will have substantially similar economic terms to Fluidstack’s agreement.

The company expects to deliver individual data halls between Q4 2026 and Q1 2027, with rent starting as each hall is handed over. Cipher attributed the revised schedule to design changes and evolving tenant requirements.

The amendment also sets out a cost-sharing arrangement. Cipher will absorb the first $359.3m of costs above the original budget. The tenant will reimburse half of further overruns through additional rent over the combined 20-year period, calculated to provide Cipher with a contracted return.

“Extending Barber Lake’s contracted life from 10 to 20 years and adding approximately $5.2 billion of contracted revenue reflects the enduring value of the infrastructure we're building,” said Tyler Page, Cipher Digital CEO.

Cipher’s original deal with Fluidstack in September 2025 covered 168MW of critical IT load. An expansion announced that November added 39MW, bringing the combined critical IT load to 207MW. Cipher said the expanded agreement covered the entire 300MW of capacity at Barber Lake.

Earlier disclosures targeted delivery of the initial 168MW phase by September 2026, followed by the additional 39MW phase by January 2027.
